title: Practical Assessment
description: Scenario questions across the whole program.

questions.question: According to the Oracle Database 19c documentation for Application Continuity for Java, which JDBC driver is required to use Application Continuity?

answerOptions.rationale: Application Continuity is explicitly built as a feature of the Oracle JDBC Thin driver.
The documentation explicitly states that Application Continuity is not supported by the JDBC OCI driver.
Application Continuity relies on Oracle-specific replay driver extensions and data source implementations unavailable in generic third-party drivers.
Application Continuity operates on client/middle-tier connections using the JDBC Thin driver infrastructure rather than internal server connections.

questions.hint: Consider which driver architecture provides client-side replay proxy capabilities without relying on native OCI C-libraries.

questions.question: Starting in Oracle Database Release 18c, which setting for the server-side service attribute FAILOVER_TYPE enables Transparent Application Continuity (TAC)?

answerOptions.rationale: Setting FAILOVER_TYPE to AUTO on the server-side service enables Transparent Application Continuity state tracking and implicit request boundaries.
FAILOVER_TYPE set to TRANSACTION configures manual Application Continuity, which requires explicit request boundary declarations.
FAILOVER_TYPE set to SELECT is used for legacy Transparent Application Failover (TAF) read queries, not Transparent Application Continuity.
FAILOVER_TYPE set to SESSION is a legacy TAF mode that reconnects the session without replaying in-flight transactional state.

questions.hint: Think of the attribute value that allows the database driver and server to automatically detect implicit request boundaries.

questions.question: In Oracle Database Release 19c, when FAILOVER_TYPE is set to AUTO on the database service, which Java system property can be set to false to explicitly turn off implicit beginRequest calls on new physical connections?

answerOptions.rationale: Setting oracle.jdbc.beginRequestAtConnectionCreation to false overrides the default 19c behavior that implicitly begins a request on physical connection creation under TAC.
This property controls session state tracking for implicit request boundaries during runtime execution, rather than connection creation initialization.
This is not a valid Oracle JDBC system property; disabling replay dynamically is handled via specific driver proxy APIs.
This property does not exist in the Application Continuity replay driver specification.

questions.hint: Focus on the property specifically named after the connection creation phase and the beginRequest action.

questions.question: Which Java interface must an application implement to create a custom connection initialization callback for re-establishing initial session state after failover?

answerOptions.rationale: Implementing oracle.jdbc.replay.ConnectionInitializationCallback allows applications to register custom logic that executes immediately following a successful reconnection.
ReplayableConnection is the interface exposed by connection proxies to manage request boundaries and retrieve statistics, not a callback creation interface.
OracleConnection is the standard vendor connection interface providing explicit request boundary methods like beginRequest and endRequest.
XAConnection is a standard JDBC interface for distributed transactions and does not contain Application Continuity callback initialization logic.

questions.hint: Look for the interface in the oracle.jdbc.replay package dedicated specifically to initialization callback routines.

questions.question: In Oracle Database 12c Release 2 (12.2.0.1) and later, what happens to Application Continuity replay on a connection once it participates in a global/XA transaction?

answerOptions.text: Replay is disabled on that connection and remains disabled until the next request begins.
answerOptions.rationale: Engaging in any XA operation disables replay protection on that physical connection for the remainder of the current request boundary.

answerOptions.text: Replay automatically resumes as soon as the connection switches back to local transaction mode within the same request.
answerOptions.rationale: Switching back from global/XA mode to local transaction mode does not automatically re-enable replay until the current request ends and a new one starts.

answerOptions.text: Replay remains active but switches automatically from manual Application Continuity to Transparent Application Continuity.
answerOptions.rationale: XA operations suspend replay capabilities entirely regardless of whether Application Continuity or TAC is configured.

answerOptions.text: Replay throws a SQLRecoverableException immediately prior to executing the XA statement.
answerOptions.rationale: XA operations execute normally without error; exception throwing only occurs if an outage happens while replay is disabled.

questions.hint: Consider how long the disabling effect of an XA boundary lasts relative to request demarcation.

questions.question: According to the Oracle Automatic Storage Management (ASM) documentation for OLTP workloads, which striping configuration and allocation unit subdivision are used for Online Redo Logs (ORLs)?

answerOptions.text: Fine-Grained Striping with 128 KB stripe sets
answerOptions.rationale: Fine-Grained Striping subdivides Allocation Units into 128 KB stripe sets across all disks to minimize latency for high-frequency write targets like ORLs.

answerOptions.text: Coarse-Grained Striping with 1 MB to 4 MB Allocation Units
answerOptions.rationale: Coarse-Grained Striping uses full Allocation Units (1 MB to 4 MB) and is targeted at large sequential files such as data files and RMAN backups.

answerOptions.text: Fine-Grained Striping with 512 KB stripe sets
answerOptions.rationale: ASM Fine-Grained Striping specifically breaks Allocation Units into 128 KB chunks, not 512 KB.

answerOptions.text: Coarse-Grained Striping with 64 KB Allocation Units
answerOptions.rationale: Coarse striping operates on full AUs (typically 1 MB or larger) rather than sub-megabyte allocations.

questions.hint: Recall which striping pattern breaks down Allocation Units into small 128 KB chunks for rapid, low-latency writes.

questions.question: Which ASM redundancy model implements 3-way mirroring across Failure Groups and requires a minimum of three Failure Groups?

answerOptions.rationale: High Redundancy enforces 3-way mirroring across ASM Failure Groups, requiring at least three separate failure domains.
Normal Redundancy enforces 2-way mirroring and requires a minimum of two Failure Groups.
External Redundancy performs no mirroring within ASM, delegating hardware fault tolerance to storage array RAID controllers.
Extended Redundancy applies to stretched clusters across sites, whereas standard 3-way mirroring within an ASM disk group is designated as High Redundancy.

questions.hint: Identify the redundancy level recommended for mission-critical setups requiring maximum fault tolerance through triple mirroring.

questions.question: In the storage architecture guidelines for IFS Applications, which ASM disk group is designated to store active data files, index tablespaces, and system tablespaces?

answerOptions.rationale: The DATA disk group serves as primary operational storage for active tablespaces, data files, indexes, and system tablespaces.
The RECO (or FRA) disk group is reserved for recovery assets, archive logs, Flashback logs, and RMAN backups.
SYSTEM is a tablespace name within the database, not an ASM disk group designation.
Archived redo logs reside inside the RECO disk group rather than a standalone ARCH disk group.

questions.hint: Distinguish between the primary operational disk group and the dedicated recovery disk group.

questions.question: According to the Real Application Clusters Administration and Deployment Guide 19c, approximately what percentage of total System Global Area (SGA) memory is consumed by the Global Resource Directory (GRD) and Cache Fusion components?

answerOptions.rationale: Oracle RAC documentation notes that GRD locks and Cache Fusion tracking structures consume approximately 10 percent of total SGA memory.
Inter-instance lock tracking requires significantly more SGA footprint than single-instance metadata structures.
A 25 percent overhead allocation exceeds the typical memory requirement noted for GCS and GES structures.
Reserving half of the SGA for resource directories would undesirably starve the Buffer Cache and Shared Pool.

questions.hint: Think of the standard memory sizing adjustment factor required when converting a single-instance SGA to Oracle RAC.

questions.question: In an active-active Oracle RAC cluster, which technology transfers cached database blocks directly between instance SGAs over the private Interconnect without writing to disk?

answerOptions.rationale: Cache Fusion coordinates memory caches across instances by transferring data blocks directly over the Interconnect network.
ASM abstracts physical disk storage into disk groups but does not handle inter-instance SGA buffer transfers.
FAN publishes cluster event notifications to client connection pools during node status changes.
Transaction Guard provides transactional commit status verification following outages rather than block transfers.

questions.hint: Focus on the high-speed memory-sharing protocol that avoids disk I/O when instances request shared data blocks.

questions.question: According to the Oracle for SAP Cloud and Infrastructure Update, what combination of technologies powers the Persistent Memory Data & Commit Accelerator in Exadata X8M-2 running Oracle Database 19c?

answerOptions.text: Intel® Optane™ modules associated with RDMA over Converged Ethernet (RoCE) 100GbE
answerOptions.rationale: Exadata X8M-2 combines Intel® Optane™ persistent memory modules with 100GbE RoCE to enable direct remote memory access.

answerOptions.text: Flash SSDs paired with InfiniBand 40GbE switches
answerOptions.rationale: InfiniBand was utilized in earlier Exadata generations prior to the introduction of RoCE and Optane PMEM in X8M.

answerOptions.text: NVMe drives managed by ASM Fine-Grained Striping
answerOptions.rationale: NVMe drives provide flash storage but do not constitute the persistent memory RDMA commit accelerator tier.

answerOptions.text: DRAM acceleration combined with TCP/IP over Public Network
answerOptions.rationale: RDMA bypasses traditional network stack protocols like TCP/IP and public network adapters.

questions.hint: Identify the high-speed Ethernet protocol and persistent memory hardware module featured in Exadata X8M models.

questions.question: In Oracle Multitenant Architecture, which container is responsible for storing Oracle system metadata, common user accounts, and global initialization parameters?

answerOptions.rationale: The root container (CDB$ROOT) manages global memory, background processes, system metadata, and common administrative users.
PDB$SEED is a read-only template pluggable database used exclusively for provisioning new PDBs.
User PDBs store application-specific schemas and data isolated from other tenant environments.
A PDB's SYSTEM tablespace contains local metadata for that specific pluggable database, not container-wide definitions.

questions.hint: Recall the top-level root container name that anchors all background processes and global metadata.

questions.question: How does a Release Update Revision (RUR) differ from a Release Update (RU) in the Oracle Database patch management lifecycle?

answerOptions.text: An RUR provides security and regression-focused patches that extend the lifespan of an existing RU without introducing new functional bug fixes.
answerOptions.rationale: RURs extend an RU's maintenance window by adding critical security and stability fixes while avoiding functional changes.

answerOptions.text: An RUR is a quarterly cumulative patch that increments the minor release version and introduces new functional feature enhancements.
answerOptions.rationale: Quarterly cumulative patches that increment the minor release version are Release Updates (RUs).

answerOptions.text: An RUR is applied only to CDB$ROOT while RUs are applied exclusively to individual PDBs.
answerOptions.rationale: Both RUs and RURs patch the binary database home shared by all containers in the multitenant architecture.

answerOptions.text: An RUR replaces major database releases every two years while RUs are issued monthly.
answerOptions.rationale: Both RU and RUR release schedules follow Oracle's quarterly patching cadence.

questions.hint: Consider which patch type focuses strictly on stability and security maintenance for an established baseline.

questions.question: When Automatic Shared Memory Management (ASMM) is enabled by setting sga_target to a non-zero value, which set of memory structures does Oracle dynamically tune?

answerOptions.text: Buffer Cache, Shared Pool, Large Pool, and Java Pool
answerOptions.rationale: ASMM dynamically adjusts allocations across the Buffer Cache, Shared Pool, Large Pool, and Java Pool based on workload demand.

answerOptions.text: Program Global Area (PGA) work areas and sort buffers
answerOptions.rationale: PGA memory is managed independently via the pga_aggregate_target parameter.

answerOptions.text: Redo Log Buffer and Process Private Memory
answerOptions.rationale: The Redo Log Buffer size is static and not dynamically sized by ASMM algorithms.

answerOptions.text: ASM Allocation Units and Cache Fusion buffers
answerOptions.rationale: ASM storage allocation and GRD metadata structures are governed by separate instance parameters.

questions.hint: Identify the primary memory pools contained within the shared System Global Area (SGA).

questions.question: What privilege must be granted to an application user in Oracle Database to retain function results for named mutable functions (such as SYSDATE or SYS_GUID) during Application Continuity replay?

answerOptions.text: KEEP DATE TIME or KEEP SYSGUID privileges
answerOptions.rationale: Granting KEEP privileges (e.g., GRANT KEEP DATE TIME TO [user]) explicitly allows the replay driver to restore original runtime values during replay.
The GRANT ALL statement explicitly excludes mutable value privileges, requiring dedicated GRANT KEEP statements.
DBMS_SERVICE manages service attributes on the database and does not grant session-level function result retention.
System configuration rights do not authorize session object mutability behavior for application SQL execution.

questions.hint: Look for the security keyword designed to 'preserve' original values across replay operations.

questions.question: What are the default values for FAILOVER_RETRIES and FAILOVER_DELAY when configuring database services for Application Continuity?

answerOptions.rationale: The standard default configuration allocates 30 retries with a 10-second delay between attempts.
This transposes the retry count and delay interval parameters.
900 seconds is the default value for REPLAY_INITIATION_TIMEOUT, not FAILOVER_RETRIES.
A 5-retry limit with 1-second delay is too short to sustain database service relocation during planned or unplanned outages.

questions.hint: Recall the parameter table where retry count is a positive integer around 30 and delay is expressed in seconds.

questions.question: What happens to the service attribute FAILOVER_RESTORE when FAILOVER_TYPE is set to AUTO on a database service in Oracle Database 18c and later?

answerOptions.text: FAILOVER_RESTORE is automatically set to AUTO and cannot be changed while FAILOVER_TYPE is AUTO.
answerOptions.rationale: Enabling Transparent Application Continuity (FAILOVER_TYPE=AUTO) automatically locks FAILOVER_RESTORE to AUTO to ensure initial state restoration.

answerOptions.text: FAILOVER_RESTORE must be manually set to LEVEL1 via SRVCTL or service creation fails.
answerOptions.rationale: LEVEL1 is used for manual Application Continuity (FAILOVER_TYPE=TRANSACTION), whereas TAC sets FAILOVER_RESTORE automatically.

answerOptions.text: FAILOVER_RESTORE defaults to NONE, disabling session state restoration.
answerOptions.rationale: NONE is the default when TAC is disabled, but enabling FAILOVER_TYPE=AUTO changes FAILOVER_RESTORE automatically.

answerOptions.text: FAILOVER_RESTORE is overridden and disabled if any application callback is registered.
answerOptions.rationale: Configured callbacks override specific restored state items, but do not set FAILOVER_RESTORE itself to disabled.

questions.hint: Consider how Transparent Application Continuity automates session restoration attributes alongside failover types.

questions.question: Which initialization parameter sets the global target for total non-shared memory allocated across all server process work areas for sort operations and hash joins?

answerOptions.rationale: pga_aggregate_target controls the total memory dedicated to private process work areas across active sessions.
sga_target manages shared memory structures accessible to all database processes.
open_cursors specifies the maximum number of open handles a session can maintain simultaneously.
processes sets the maximum number of operating system user processes that can connect concurrently.

questions.hint: Look for the parameter governing aggregate Program Global Area limits.

questions.question: Which command-line utility is used in Oracle RAC to manage cluster services, database resources, and server pool configurations?

answerOptions.rationale: Server Control Utility (SRVCTL) is the standard administrative tool for managing RAC database resources, services, and server pools.
Recovery Manager (RMAN) handles database backup, restore, and duplicate operations.
ORADIM is a Windows-specific command-line tool used to control Oracle background services.
ASMCMD is dedicated to administering files and directories within ASM disk groups.

questions.hint: Identify the primary utility acronym representing the Server Control tool.

questions.question: During a RAC node failover workflow using Application Continuity, what component does the client driver query on a surviving instance using the session's assigned LTXID to check if an in-flight transaction committed?

answerOptions.rationale: The driver queries Transaction Guard on a surviving instance using the Logical Transaction ID (LTXID) to verify commit outcome.
GRD tracks lock states across active instances but does not evaluate client transactional commit outcomes during failover.
ONS delivers Fast Application Notification (FAN) event messages to connection pools rather than checking commit states.
AWR collects historical performance statistics and snapshot metrics, playing no role in runtime failover validation.

questions.hint: Think of the Oracle feature required as a prerequisite for Application Continuity to guarantee transaction outcome certainty.
